extra_misconceptions.fact: Intact skin over a friction blister forms a sterile barrier against waterborne bacteria and should be protected with a moleskin doughnut pad.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Popping a friction blister on a rower's palm with an unsterilized pin speeds up skin healing on campouts.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Water conducts heat twenty-five times faster than air, causing hypothermia even in seventy-degree water during prolonged immersion.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hypothermia only occurs when air and water temperatures drop below fifty degrees Fahrenheit.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Sustained rowing exertion causes steady fluid loss through respiration and sweat regardless of cloud cover, requiring regular water intake.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rowers cannot become dehydrated on cool or overcast days because sweat evaporates more slowly.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rubbing cold-damaged tissue causes mechanical cellular injury; warm affected hands gradually against the torso or in warm water instead.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Vigorous rubbing of frostbitten or cold-numbed fingers restores circulation safely after cold-water rowing.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a rowboat's stability when wind waves strike the hull broadside in open water?
Which physical indicator distinguishes heat exhaustion from life-threatening heatstroke on the water?
Under what condition does cold-water immersion trigger an involuntary gasp reflex before hypothermia sets in?
Why is it dangerous to remain on open water for even ten minutes after hearing distant thunder?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The first seventy-five yards require a strong stroke like sidestroke, breaststroke, trudgen, or crawl rather than an exhausting dog paddle.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Completing a hundred yards of dog paddling satisfies the forward-stroke portion of the Scouting America swimmer test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The entire hundred-yard distance and transition into the elementary backstroke must be swum continuously without resting on walls or lanes.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Touching the pool wall to catch your breath for thirty seconds is permitted during the hundred-yard swimmer test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Swimmer classifications must be renewed annually so counselors can verify current physical stamina and water competence before boating.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Passing the Scouting America swimmer classification test once at summer camp qualifies a Scout permanently for all future years.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The post-swim phase requires floating on the back with minimal motion to demonstrate energy-conserving survival skills in deep water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Treading water vigorously with high leg kicks is the required technique for the one-minute post-swim survival phase.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms the water depth is sufficient for the feetfirst jump in the swimmer test?
Why is it dangerous to allow a swimmer to push off the bottom during the hundred-yard continuous swim?
Which stroke mechanics must a Scout demonstrate during the final twenty-five yards of the swimmer test?
What happens to a Scout's energy reserves if they thrash instead of floating calmly during the resting phase?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Safety Afloat rules require every person in a rowboat to wear a properly fitted Coast Guard approved life jacket at all times.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Strong swimmers who passed the swimmer test only need to carry a throwable cushion on board a rowboat.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An oversized life jacket rides up around a small swimmer's head in the water, obstructing breathing instead of keeping the chin above waves.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Buying an oversized adult life jacket for a small Scout provides extra buoyancy and safer flotation.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Type III vests offer wide arm cutouts for comfortable rowing mobility, but they require conscious movement to keep the wearer face-up.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Type III paddling vests automatically turn an unconscious swimmer face-up in rough open water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Direct high heat melts internal flotation foam and weakens nylon webbing, so life jackets must always air-dry out of direct sunlight.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Drying wet life jackets directly over a campfire or radiator preserves the foam buoyancy material.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms that a life jacket will not ride up over a rower's chin and ears in the water?
Why is it dangerous to store a buckled life jacket underneath a rower's seat instead of wearing it?
Which physical indicator on a life jacket's inner label verifies United States Coast Guard approval and sizing?
What happens to a rower's stroke length when a bulky life jacket restricts shoulder and arm rotation?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The leg drive against the foot stretchers generates the majority of stroke power, while the back and arms transfer that force to the handles.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rowing power in a sliding-seat shell comes primarily from pulling the oar handles with the biceps.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Steering straight requires lining up two stationary landmarks behind the stern and glancing over your shoulder only occasionally for hazards.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Looking over your shoulder every two strokes is the most accurate way to steer a straight course.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Submerging only the oar blade just beneath the surface maximizes horizontal leverage and allows a clean release at the finish.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Burying the entire oar shaft deep beneath the surface produces stronger forward thrust during the drive.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pulling one oar while simultaneously backing water with the other spins the hull tightly around its center without forward drift.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pivoting a rowboat in place requires dragging one oar passively while pulling hard with the opposite oar.

extra_socratic_questions: Which visual alignment method keeps a rowboat traveling in a straight hundred-yard line without constant turning?
What happens to the rowboat's turning radius when a rower pulls with one oar while backing water with the other?
Under what condition does feathering the oar blades during the recovery phase prevent catching a crab?
Where should a Scout position the oar blades in the water to bring a moving rowboat to a controlled stop?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Stepping on the gunwale rolls the hull violently toward the dock; passengers must step directly onto the centerline keel while crouching low.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stepping onto the wooden gunwale first gives a passenger the best leverage when boarding a rowboat from a pier.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Stern sculling uses a continuous figure-eight motion with the blade pitched at forty-five degrees to generate steady forward thrust.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sculling over the stern propels a rowboat by sweeping the oar blade back and forth like a canoe paddle.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Approaching into the wind or current acts as a natural brake, allowing the rower to regulate speed and settle gently alongside the pier.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Approaching a pier with strong wind and current behind the stern provides the easiest docking control.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Only one person moves at a time while keeping their center of gravity low and holding both gunwales as the other sits centered on the bottom.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Two occupants changing seats in a rowboat should walk past each other while standing upright for balance.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position their feet and hands when stepping from a low pier into a fixed-seat rowboat?
What happens to forward propulsion during stern sculling if the oar blade remains flat instead of angled?
Why is it dangerous to stand upright simultaneously with a passenger while switching seats in open water?
Under what condition does approaching a dock into the wind or current improve a rower's boat control?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Recreational rowboats contain built-in flotation chambers or buoyant materials that keep a swamped hull and its crew afloat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A rowboat filled to the gunwales with water loses all buoyancy and sinks straight to the lake bottom.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Distances across open water are deceptive, and a large swamped boat is far easier for rescuers to spot than a lone swimmer's head.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Swimming for a shoreline that looks close is safer than waiting beside a swamped rowboat in cold water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A water-filled hull has almost no roll stability, so occupants must sit low on the bottom boards to prevent an immediate second capsize.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Standing on the thwarts after reboarding a swamped rowboat keeps a Scout warmer while paddling to shore.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Reaching across the overturned bottom to pull the far gunwale toward you rolls the hull upright using your body weight as leverage.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Righting an overturned rowboat requires lifting one gunwale straight up into the air from deep water.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to abandon a swamped rowboat and attempt to swim toward a distant shoreline?
Where should a Scout position their body weight when reboarding a swamped rowboat in deep water?
What happens to the freeboard of a swamped rowboat if two Scouts climb over the same gunwale together?
Which technique allows a Scout inside a water-filled hull to make steady headway toward shore?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Approaching bow-first risks striking the swimmer; stopping short and pivoting the stern toward them gives the rower clear visibility.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Approaching a panicked swimmer bow-first at full rowing speed gets them out of the water fastest.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Hauling heavy weight over the side gunwale easily capsizes a rowboat, whereas towing a conscious swimmer at the stern preserves stability.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling an exhausted swimmer directly over the midship gunwale is the safest way to complete a rowboat rescue.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A panicked swimmer can yank an unshipped oar out of the rower's hands or pull the side of the boat over, leaving the rescuer stranded.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Extending an oar tip to a panicked swimmer in deep water is safer than maneuvering the stern within reach.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Calling out calm, clear instructions during the approach reassures the swimmer and prepares them to grasp the stern transom safely.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The rower should remain silent during the twenty-yard approach to focus entirely on stroke cadence.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to let a tired swimmer grab the side gunwale or oar blade during a rowboat rescue?
Where should a Scout position the rowboat's stern before instructing a distressed swimmer to make contact?
What happens to the rower's line of sight once the swimmer holds the stern for the tow back to shore?
Under what condition does a rowing rescue take priority over entering the water for a swimming rescue?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A metal pin passing through the oar shaft locks a Northridge oarlock at a fixed angle, preventing the rower from feathering the blade.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pinned Northridge oarlocks allow a rower to rotate and feather the oar blade freely at the end of each stroke.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Aluminum hulls resist rot and UV degradation without varnish, though they conduct water temperature rapidly and can loosen rivets on rocks.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Aluminum rowboats require annual sanding and varnishing to prevent rot in freshwater environments.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A closed ring oarlock traps the oar collar until the handle is slid all the way through the ring, which slows down emergency oar stowing.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Ring oarlocks with leather buttons permit an oar to be lifted straight up and stowed inside the boat instantly.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Competitive shells use ultra-narrow carbon-fiber or composite hulls with outriggers and sliding seats to minimize hydrodynamic drag.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Competitive rowing shells use wide, flat-bottomed wooden hulls to maximize cargo capacity and wave stability.

extra_socratic_questions: Which oarlock design allows a recreational rower to feather the blade while preventing the oar from slipping free?
What happens to an unpinned oar in an open-horn oarlock if the rower releases the handle on rough water?
Under what condition does an aluminum rowboat require extra seam inspection compared to a molded fiberglass hull?
What structural feature distinguishes a competitive sliding-seat sculling shell from a heavy commercial dory?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rotating the blade flat before extracting it pushes the hull downward and causes a crab; feather only after the blade clears the water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Feathering the oar blade underwater before the stroke finishes increases hull speed by slicing cleanly out of the wake.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Taking heavy waves on the beam risks swamping or capsizing the boat; keep weight low and angle the bow at 45 degrees into the waves.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rowing parallel to breaking waves in a windstorm keeps the hull level and reaches shelter faster than angling into the chop.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Upright hulls trap rainwater and snowmelt that freeze and crack seams; store the boat upside down on padded racks with plugs removed.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Storing a rowboat upright on flat ground with the drain plug sealed protects the hull interior from winter moisture damage.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Proper oar length depends on the span between oarlocks, typically twice the beam span plus two feet, so the handles clear the rower.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Selecting the longest available oars always gives a rower better leverage and higher cruising speed in any open rowboat.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to forward hull momentum and blade clearance when a rower keeps the oar blades squared against a strong headwind?
Why is it dangerous to let a rowboat turn broadside into the trough of steep waves instead of quartering the bow into the wind?
What measurement between the oarlocks across the hull beam is used to calculate the proper oar length for a fixed-seat rowboat?
Which physical indicator on wooden gunwales, oarlocks, or hull seams signals that a stored rowboat needs repair before launch?
